extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and patent agents/attorneys seeking national patent-law requirements
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes country-by-country statutory standards and procedural requirements for obtaining, maintaining, and invalidating patents (what is patentable, required application contents, term options, fees/annuities, working/put-into-practice requirements, grounds for nullity, assignment/registration, publication/opposition, and enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Working/put-into-practice requirement (forfeiture for non-use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent rights can be forfeited or become void if the invention is not put into practice within a specified period (commonly one, two, or three years from grant or from commencement of term) or when working is suspended/abandoned for more than a specified period (commonly one or two years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hawaii/other (not put into practice within a year from grant or abandoned for more than a year); Italy: patents ≤5 years must be put in operation within first year; patents >5 years have two years to work; Japan: not practically applied within three years or working suspended for three years; Mexico: not put into operation within two years or working interrupted for two years; Norway: must be put into operation within three years and not discontinued for one year. 'Want of funds' is generally not accepted as valid excuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be novel; an invention is not considered new if it has been previously published or put into public use (subject to specific country exceptions regarding short exhibition periods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy: 'The invention must be novel.' Norway: prior knowledge enabling experts to carry it out destroys novelty; publication/exhibition for ≤6 months prior to application may not prevent grant. Peru/Portugal/Russia/Mexico list novelty as ground for nullity. Foreign patents and public use/importation before application can bar patentability in many jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject-matter definitions (Italy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions considered patentable have as their immediate object: (1) an industrial product or result; (2) any instrument, machine, etc., or mechanical arrangement; (3) any process or method of industrial production; (4) a motor, or the industrial application of a force already known; (5) the technical application of a scientific principle producing direct industrial results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets scope of protectable inventions in Italy; novelty and utility still required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express exclusions of subject-matter (country-specific)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain subject-matter categories are expressly non-patentable in particular countries (e.g., articles of food, drink, fashion, or medicine in Japan; pharmaceutical compositions, estate-working plans, financial combinations, and known motors applied to known industrial purposes in Mexico; munitions of war in Russia except when adapted to other purposes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also: Peru and Portugal exclude theoretical/scientific principles without indicated industrial application, and other public-order or policy-based exclusions are noted. Check the specific national provision for exact exclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application content: specification, drawings, models, and specimens
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications must include a full specification and, where applicable, full drawings and, if required, a complete model; for compositions, specimens of ingredients sufficient for experiment must be furnished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Country examples: Italy (three copies of description in French or Italian; drawings/models), Hawaii (full specification, drawings, complete model if required), Japan (three copies of specification with drawings), Mexico (description in Spanish, drawings in ink to scale, duplicate), Russia (exact description with plans and drawings; models often required for firearms/surgical instruments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal application particulars (identity, title, term requested)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application must state the name, surname and residence of the applicant (and attorney/agent), a short and precise description/title of the nature and object of the discovery, and the length of the term desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit in Italy and other jurisdictions; some countries require power of attorney legalized by a consul, receipts for taxes, and lists of accompanying documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions and supporting documents must be submitted in the prescribed language(s) and signed by the inventor or attorney; alterations/corrections may be forbidden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy requires French or Italian; Mexico requires Spanish and 'without alterations or corrections'; Luxembourg requires French or German; Japan requires signatures of all persons connected with the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication, inspection, and publication schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: After grant (or after a set period), drawings and descriptions are published and records of patents and changes are made public; periodic lists and catalogs of granted patents are published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy publishes drawings/descriptions three months after grant and issues quarterly and semiannual lists; Mexico publishes grants in official journals and issues an annual catalogue; Luxembourg publishes records; Norway advertises applications and opens them for public inspection for eight weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition and public objection periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications or granted patents are subject to public opposition or objections within specified time windows following publication or advertisement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mexico allows oppositions within two months from publication; Norway opens papers for eight weeks for opposition; procedural review/appeal mechanisms exist (e.g., Patent Commission and superior commissions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination scope (substantive vs. formal examinations vary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some jurisdictions perform substantive examinations into novelty/merit, others grant patents without substantive examination, leaving validity at applicants' risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Russia and Norway conduct novelty/merit investigations; Luxembourg and Paraguay grant patents without examination 'at the risk of the applicants'; Italy generally subjects certain classes (e.g., food/drink) to sanitary council review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration/term options and measurement of term
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are granted for country-specific terms (various options such as 1–15 years, commonly 5, 6, 10, 15), and the commencement/measurement of duration is prescribed (from date of application, grant, or next quarterly date following application).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy 1–15 years (duration counted from next quarter month after application); Japan 5/10/15 years; Russia options of 3/5/10 years; Mexico 6 or 10 years; Luxembourg 15 years; many countries allow applicant to choose term within statutory range. Some imported-invention patents cannot extend beyond foreign patent expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annuities, taxes, fees, and payment timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintenance of patent rights requires payment of proportional taxes and annual annuities; amounts, schedules, and payment-in-advance requirements vary by country and nonpayment within grace periods leads to forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy requires proportional tax and annual annuities with three months' grace; Luxembourg has annual tax with three-month default rule; Russia and Norway list government charges; payments often due at application and on set quarterly/annual dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace periods and consequences of late payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Some laws provide short grace periods for annuity/tax payment (commonly three months) after which the patent is forfeited; some jurisdictions do not admit grace for prolongation payments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy allows three months' grace for annuities (not for prolongation); Luxembourg and others specify three months' default period; check local rules for remedies or reinstatement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of addition / patents of addition (improvements)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certificates/patents of addition are granted for improvements and are annexed to or expire with the principal patent; priority/preference rules and eligibility vary (often original inventor or assigns have priority in initial period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy grants certificates of addition annexed to principal patent; Mexico grants patents of addition to improvements and restricts them to original inventor/assigns for the first year; Luxembourg and Norway provide patents of addition expiring with original.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certificates of reduction / disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees may request reduction/disclaimer of patent scope within specified early months (e.g., first six months) to limit the patent to one or more parts or to point out parts excluded from the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy allows certificates of reduction within first six months with specified fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction to single subject-matter per patent
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent will not be allowed to comprise more than one subject-matter of invention (claims must be limited to one principal object and necessary accessories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly noted in Portugal and Mexico (application must be limited to one principal object).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to state claims (definite statement of invention to be protected)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must conclude with a definite statement of what the applicant considers to be his invention and wishes to protect (i.e., express claims).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express requirement in Norway and Russia; used by examiners/commissions to determine scope and for publication/advertising prior to opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment, transfer, registration and effect against third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: All deeds of transfer, assignment, licences, and dealings with patents must be registered; assignments are not effective against third parties until registration date in the Patent Office (or within prescribed time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy, Liberia, Luxembourg, Norway require registration; unregistered assignments may not bind third parties; publicity/registration costs and procedures vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for nullity or voiding of patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents become void or may be annulled for enumerated grounds: invention not new or useful; description insufficient to enable carrying out the invention; title fraudulent; invention proscribed by law; tax/annuity not paid; patent granted to other than inventor; introduction of patented articles from abroad (in some jurisdictions); or other statutory causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy lists eight specific causes (including insufficient description, lack of novelty/utility, tax nonpayment, not worked); Mexico, Peru, Portugal, Luxembourg, and others provide similar enumerated grounds. Procedures to demand nullity often involve administrative ministry or court.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importation of articles made abroad and effect on patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: In many jurisdictions, articles made according to the patented invention and imported into the country do not necessarily invalidate the patent; however, importation and sale by others may lead to forfeiture if the patentee ignores infringement or fails to act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Several countries state 'Articles made abroad according to the invention can be imported without rendering the patent invalid' (Italy, Luxembourg, Norway). Japan and others provide that patents may become void when patented articles are imported and sold and the patentee ignores such importation/sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marking/labeling requirement to recover damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Patented articles must bear a mark settled by the Minister or indicate 'Patented' (and similar legends) and failure to mark may prevent recovery of damages from infringers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Japan requires a mark settled by the Minister; Mexico requires 'Patented' and 'Sans garantie du Gouvernement' legends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government use and compulsory appropriation with compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Government may use patented inventions for public service or appropriate patented inventions of essential value to industry/private use, but compensation to the patentee is required, to be fixed or settled by arbitration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norway and Russia explicitly allow government use subject to compensation; Russia may reserve rights for state use of certain inventions (e.g., munitions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal and civil remedies for infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringers may be liable to civil damages and/or criminal penalties (fines and imprisonment) depending on jurisdiction and statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Japan: infringers liable to imprisonment not exceeding one year and fines up to specified amounts; Luxembourg prescribes penalties and fines; civil suits for damages are common (e.g., Liberia Supreme Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Commission / examination bodies and appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The examination and decision upon patent applications rests with administrative/expert bodies (e.g., Patent Commission) whose decisions may be reviewed, reconsidered, or appealed to superior commissions or courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norway: Patent Commission with president and five expert members; appeals to superior Patent Commission. Italy uses Minister and sanitary council for certain classes; Russia uses governmental bodies with administrative processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority caveat / temporary priority filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventors may file a caveat or similar temporary document kept secret to secure priority for a limited period (commonly one year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hawaii/other provisions allow filing of caveat giving priority for one year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for foreign-patented inventions (conditions and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Foreign patents may afford the right to obtain a patent domestically if the domestic application is made before expiration of the foreign patent and before importation or public use domestically; the domestic patent term may be limited by the foreign patent's remaining term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy and Mexico permit domestic patents for inventions already patented abroad if application made before foreign patent expiration and before domestic import/use; Italy limits duration so it does not exceed maximum national term and may tie expiry to foreign patent expiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration and publication of records (assignments, changes, extracts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Records of deposit, changes, additions, cancellations, or assignment of patents are kept and published; certified extracts may be obtained at applicant's expense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy, Luxembourg, and other countries publish such records and supply extracts on stamped paper or for fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence of working: third-party manufacture or advertisement as sufficient working
rubrics_metrics.description: In some jurisdictions, manufacture by an independent person according to the specification or advertisements may be considered sufficient evidence of working the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portugal explicitly notes an independent person's manufacture in accordance with specification is sufficient working, and newspaper advertisements are held to be sufficient evidence of subsequent workings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant identity and residence requirements (non-residents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-resident applicants may be required to appoint a resident attorney or agent to represent them and must comply with additional formalities (e.g., legalized power of attorney).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Norway requires a resident attorney for non-residents; Italy requires legalized power of attorney by Consul of Italy; other countries impose similar representation requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special sanitary or technical review for particular classes
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain classes of inventions (e.g., drinks and eatables) may be subject to review by specialized councils (e.g., Superior Sanitary Council) before grant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy references sanitary council review for patents for drinks and eatables; other states may have analogous specialist reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on importer/introducer rights
rubrics_metrics.description: An importer who is not the inventor may receive only limited-duration patents (shorter terms) in some jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portugal grants an importer (not the inventor) a patent only for five years; Mexico grants patents to first introducer but with specific rules; Russia grants importation patents for limited years not beyond foreign patent expiry.
